item.title: Polanski makes his mark as Labour candidate fails to attend election hustings. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Polanski makes his mark as Labour candidate fails to attend election hustings

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Wed, 09/23/2026 - 16:01
Green Party leader speaks confidently at Holborn and St Pancras meeting, but Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali is nowhere to be seen
Green Party leader Zack Polanski (R) and Liberal Democrat candidate Patrick Stillman (L) speak at Holborn and St Pancras hustings at the P21 gallery on Tuesday 22 September 2026 (Imran Mulla/MEE)
Off

On Tuesday evening, a five-minute walk from King's Cross train station, Green Party leader Zack Polanski strode into an art gallery to speak at a campaign hustings.

But his main rival in the UK parliamentary by-election for Holborn and St Pancras, the Labour Party candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, didn't turn up.

"I'm not surprised," one former Labour councillor grumbled. He said he knew Abdi-Wali personally. His wife alleged that "she just does whatever the bosses tell her. She can't do policy". Labour's candidate was scared of being asked tough questions, both of them believed.  

Mahad, a local resident and pro-Palestine campaigner of Somali heritage, also said he wasn't surprised that Abdi-Wali skipped the hustings, suggesting she might want to avoid scrutiny of her views on Israel and Palestine.

The hustings was arranged by the Camden Muslim Network, which was founded in 2024. Organisers told Middle East Eye that the Labour team said Abdi-Wali couldn't attend because of another commitment.

But there was widespread discontent in the gallery. Hustings, conventionally, are supposed to allow candidates to pitch themselves to local residents but also to allow residents to press and scrutinise them. 

A Green Party source said the hustings "were an opportunity to discuss the issues that matter to voters, from Gaza and conflicts in the Middle East to local issues of concern".

"You’d have thought Labour would at least have had the courtesy and respect to explain its position on these issues to voters," they added. 

MEE contacted Abdi-Wali to ask why she had not attended but did not receive a reply.

'You'd have thought Labour would at least have had the courtesy and respect to explain its position'

- Green Party source

The Camden Muslim Network is openly pro-Palestine. It backed Andrew Feinstein, an independent pro-Palestine candidate, in the 2024 general election.

Feinstein, a former Afican National Congress (ANC) MP in South Africa, received more than 7,000 votes, slashing the majority previously enjoyed by Keir Starmer, who nonetheless retained the seat and became prime minister.

It was Starmer's resignation as an MP - shortly after he was forced out of Downing Street - that triggered this by-election in the London seat.

This seat, which contains much of the London borough of Camden, has been staunchly Labour for decades. Could that now change?

High stakes and everything to play for

Both Labour and the Green Party are taking this by-election very seriously.

In February, in Greater Manchester's Gorton and Denton, the Greens proved they could win in a seat where they had previously had little presence.

Then Andy Burnham won the by-election in Makerfield, another seat in northwest England, sending him to Westminster and triggering Starmer's resignation.

The Green Party has been accused of sectarianism. This is why that's wrong
Read More »

Now this contest in Holborn and St Pancras is ramping up. For Labour, it is a temperature check - a test of whether the party is able to win back left-wing voters it lost under Starmer.

If the party wins the seat, Labour insiders say, Burnham could be emboldened to call a snap election. 

Ministers have been out campaigning. Abdi-Wali, the candidate, is well known in the area as the leader of Camden council. 

Meanwhile, the Green Party faces enormous questions about its future.

The left-wing party surged in the polls last year after Polanski was elected leader, gained further momentum and credibility with the Gorton and Denton victory and then took more votes from Labour in the May local elections than Reform did. 

Polanski is at least partially responsible for Starmer's downfall and Burnham's premiership.

But the Greens have their work cut out for them with a much more popular prime minister who has taken steps to address key grievances Labour voters who moved to the Greens had under Starmer.

Greens quietly optimistic

The Green Party is taking a considerable risk in this contest. The Labour government's recent comprehensive sanctions on Israeli settlements have drawn praise from the left and Palestinian solidarity groups.

If Polanski, who sits on the London Assembly but has never been an MP, fails to beat the Labour candidate, it will strike a deadly blow to the his party's image and momentum. 

But if the 43-year-old wins, it will prove the Greens still have significant support and potential to grow. 

It will send Labour the message that this volatile period isn't over and that even their London seats are not safe. 

UK settlements ban: How conspiracy theory accusing Burnham of courting 'Islamist voters' went global
Read More »

Moreover, with Polanski in parliament, the Greens' ability to act as a powerful bloc helping to shape day-to-day political discourse will be significantly boosted.

There is a great deal at stake. A senior Green source told MEE they are quietly optimistic. The party has mustered an impressive ground campaign and is receiving positive responses on the doorstep.

Holborn and St Pancras is a diverse constituency, with both affluent and working-class areas. It has around 110,000 residents and is disproportionately young (there is a large student population) and ethnically diverse - around 10 percent are of Bangladeshi origin.

There is also a sizeable Somali-origin population and around one in five voters are Muslim. This sort of diversity in different areas across the country has been traditionally advantageous for Labour, but more recently has produced significant support for the Greens.

For local resident Mahad, the change in prime minister has led to "better rhetoric", but hasn't convinced him to vote Labour.

"Labour locally have been pretty bad," Mahad said. "They've been terrible on housing, terrible on homelessness."

He described Polanski as "charismatic" and "pro-Palestine".

'Too scared to be put on the spot'

Diana Foster is the founding director of the People's Museum in Somers Town, near King's Cross, which aims to preserve the area's working class heritage. 

She said she suspected the Labour candidate was "too scared to be put on the spot". Her friend, a woman named Esther, agreed.

"The main issue is housing," said Esther, who thinks the Green Party is more in touch with pressing local concerns.

But the Greens are also campaigning heavily on foreign policy. "Gaza is a big issue," Foster said.

'Labour locally have been pretty bad. They've been terrible on housing, terrible on homelessness'

- Mahad, local resident

Both were lifelong Labour voters, but seriously disenchanted. They agreed that the change in prime minister wouldn't be enough to make them vote Labour, because the party locally hadn't changed. 

But what did Foster think of Polanski? "He's a media personality. Sagal is locally rooted, Zack has been helicoptered in."

Abdi-Wali's own story is highly unusual: she came to the UK as a child refugee from Somalia and has been hugely successful in local politics and community work.

She wears a headscarf and was attacked by Reform UK politician Zia Yusuf on social media earlier this month, for which Labour MPs accused him of racism. 

"The frontrunner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour... was born in Somalia," Yusuf declared in a post on X. "Do you understand what's happening?"

Speaking to the New Statesman this week, Abdi-Wali promised: "I will never be just another Labour backbencher... I will be someone who’s a local, committed, dedicated public servant, which I don’t think any of the other people on the ballot can be."

'He's doing something different'

But Abdi-Wali is known to have been a Starmer ally and is unpopular among local pro-Palestine activists because Camden council has resisted calls to divest from companies allegedly complicit in Israel's Gaza genocide.

One man of Bangladeshi origin told MEE that while local Bangladeshis have traditionally supported Labour, there was a strong chance many would turn to the Greens, in no small part because of Labour's record on Gaza.

'It's important that we elect MPs in Parliament who will not warmonger, but who speak for peace'

 - Zack Polanski, Green Party leader

Meanwhile, Polanski has been posting campaign videos in foreign languages - Urdu, French and Bangla.

"I think the videos are copying the New York mayor," Mahad speculated, referring to Zohran Mamdani, who is renowned for his videos speaking foreign languages in an impeccable accent.

Polanski has been mocked online for his pronunciation and attacked by political opponents for using foreign languages, particularly since very few Camden residents speak Urdu as their main language.

But some people MEE spoke to were sympathetic and even impressed by the Green leader's efforts. 

"It's a really good idea" to put out the videos, said a former Labour councillor. "It's excellent. He's doing something different."

There were about 60 people at the hustings - a mixture of age groups and ethnicities. A handful of people were visibly Muslim. 

In the end, apart from Polanski, the only other candidate to show up was Patrick Stillman of the Liberal Democrats, who have councillors in affluent areas in the north of the seat. He and Polanski were friendly with each other the entire time, with their criticisms focused on Labour.

Both candidates received regular rounds of applause for their answers. 

In Ilford North, Leanne Mohamad and the British left set their sights on Labour
Read More »

The event was notable for the absences: organisers told MEE they had invited the Conservative and Reform candidates, as well as a representative from George Galloway's Workers Party.

Galloway, who is reportedly in South Africa, is running as his own party's candidate in Holborn and St Pancras.

Generally, voters at the hustings didn't mention Galloway, seeing the by-election as a two-way contest between Labour and the Greens. 

But one person expressed concern that a small number of "elderly members" of the Muslim community could vote for Galloway, which might damage the Greens.

Local, national and foreign policy issues

Much of the actual hustings focused on local issues, including parking places and housing.

Polanski seemed well-versed on local details but generally linked local issues to broader, national ones like inequality, calling on the government "to tax multi-millionaires and billionaires a small amount to make sure that we're putting that money into our communities".

'Voices like mine or anti-war voices get ridiculed, or the media try and present us as if we're some sort of threat'

- Zack Polanski

Audience members asked about foreign policy. One man declared that "as a Jewish anti-Zionist, I dissociate myself completely with the actions of the state of Israel and with the state of Israel itself". He asked whether Israel as a whole should be sanctioned.

Stillman, the Liberal Democrat candidate, said that sanctions "shouldn't be used as a sort of hammer and nail approach, and should be a screw which you're able to turn, because that's what enables diplomatic dialogue to keep going."

Polanski struck a different tone by condemning the Labour government as "deeply cynical" for continuing to "sell arms to Israel".

He argued that "we need a full boycott divestment sanctions on goods and not just some services, but all services until Israel stops killing innocent people and stops the genocide". 

Another person asked whether Iran should have a nuclear weapon, after which a disgruntled audience member exclaimed: "Can we have some local issues?"

Polanski responded that no countries should have nuclear weapons. But he also addressed the issue of whether candidates should speak about foreign policy, arguing that "it's important that we elect MPs in parliament who will not warmonger, but who speak for peace and democracy and diplomacy".

"And what we see over and over again is voices like mine or anti-war voices get ridiculed, or the media try and present us as if we're some sort of threat or danger," he said. 

Debunked: Why Tory claims of UK extremism ‘cover-up’ fail to add up
Read More »

"I think the threat or the danger are MPs who take money off the arms trade companies and then in parliament whip up things into storms as opposed to talking about peace and diplomacy, which is ultimately what we need to be pushing for."

Both candidates spoke fluently and coherently. But the Labour candidate's absence was glaring.

It is possible that Labour believes it has a strong chance of winning and its priority is to avoid any scandals or unfortunate viral videos that could result from events like this one, and this explains its approach.

It is, after all, Labour's seat to lose. And the Greens are putting up a serious fight. But will it be possible for Labour to continue avoiding confrontation?

The actual vote is on 8 October. In between it lies both the Labour and Green conferences. A great amount could still change.

item.title: When silence has a language. [ tbsnews ]
Modernizing the shipping sector. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The government’s renewed push to modernize the shipping sector, including digitalizing vessel registration, strengthening safety protocols, and upgrading port operations, is certainly a step in the right direction as far as economic development goes.
Our economy depends heavily on maritime routes for the majority of our external trade, yet the infrastructure, regulatory systems, and fleet capacity that support this have been woeful.
To that end, the recognition that we cannot continue to lag behind global standards is long overdue, and must be treated as the beginning of a much-needed transformation.
The shipping sector has long suffered from chronic weaknesses such as outdated vessels, slow regulatory processes, and fragmented oversight among multiple agencies. These gaps have made navigation risky, slowed cargo movement, and increased costs for both exporters and importers.
In a country that must expand its export basket and find newer avenues to compete globally, inefficiency at ports and waterways is nothing if not a structural barrier to potential growth.
For decades, manual processes have enabled delays, irregularities, and unsafe vessels to operate unchecked. Thus, a transparent, technology‑driven system should reduce corruption and improve compliance,
When it comes to port modernization, we must adopt global best practices in logistics, automation, and container handling. Faster turnaround times and improved efficiency will directly strengthen our competitiveness, especially as we seek to attract higher‑value industries.
All of the modernization efforts must keep safety as a principal component. Bangladesh has witnessed too many tragic accidents on its waterways and as such, modernization must include strict enforcement of safety standards, proper training for crews, and accountability for operators who violate rules. A modern shipping sector, beyond being efficient, must first and foremost be safe.
Bangladesh, despite the challenges, continues to have significant economic ambitions, and a strong, efficient, and safe shipping sector will play a major role in ensuring those ambitions are met.

Rights for the deaf. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As the world marks the UN International Day of Sign Languages, Bangladesh must contend with a painful truth: Millions of deaf citizens continue to live without meaningful access to communication, education, healthcare, or justice.
The scale is enormous: An estimated 9.6% of Bangladesh’s population are deaf or hard of hearing. Hearing loss affects 34.6% of the population, and profound deafness affects 1.2%, with rural and low‑income communities suffering disproportionately.
That most cases arise from preventable causes is no surprise; chronic ear infections, poor sanitation, and lack of early treatment are all therefore failures of public health, not fate.
Deaf people continue to struggle accessing interpreters in hospitals, courts, police stations, and schools. Teacher training remains inadequate, with sign language rarely used in public services and employment barriers keeping many deaf individuals trapped in poverty.
This gap between recognition and reality is nothing if not a violation of rights. Sign languages are essential for full participation in society -- without them, deaf people are denied equal access to information, education, and civic life.
Our own disability laws mandate the development and use of sign language in public institutions, yet implementation remains inconsistent and negligible.
We cannot brush aside the rights of the deaf. Millions of citizens should not be deprived of essential services that everyday people take for granted. Integrating sign language therefore is critical if we are to truly progress as a nation. No hospital, school, or government office should be allowed to ignore these requirements.
Asking for equal access in their own country is not special treatment nor favours. We must commit to turning recognition into real rights, and silence into inclusion. Every citizen is entitled to that.

item.title: Sri Lanka convicts 14 over Easter Sunday massacre. [ dawn ]
item.description:
COLOMBO: Sri Lanka’s High Court convicted on Tuesday 14 of the 24 men accused of being directly involved in the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings, which killed 279 people.

The three-judge bench found that 14 of the accused were guilty on all charges, which included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms and explosives under the Prevention of Terrorism Act. A 15th defendant was found guilty of only some of the charges, while nine others were acquitted.

The presiding judge told a packed courtroom that sentencing would take place later on Tuesday. Dozens of police commandos provided security outside as the verdicts were read.

The 24 men were accused of aiding and abetting the suicide bombers who struck three luxury hotels and three churches on April 21, 2019, killing 279 people, including 45 foreigners.

Country’s historic trial brings record 23,270 charges

Local media has said some could face the death penalty, although Sri Lanka has not carried out an execution since 1976 and capital punishment is typically commuted to life imprisonment. Sri Lanka’s Roman Catholic Church welcomed the convictions.

“Finally, we have justice,” Catholic priest Jude Fernando said. “It has taken a long time to get to this point.” Teresa Fernando, a survivor who suffered head injuries, said no one should have to endure what she had gone through. “We came here today as victims of this attack to receive justice,” she said.

“Whatever the court says… we will bow our heads and accept it.” It was the first criminal prosecution directly linked to the coordinated bombings, though a former police chief and an ex-security chief were sentenced to death in July for criminal negligence after failing to prevent the attacks despite prior intelligence warnings.

All of the accused are from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community. Twenty-five men were originally cha­rged, but one defendant died in custody. Investigators blamed the attack on a homegrown extremist group.

The trial had already made Sri Lankan legal history, with prosecutors filing 23,270 charges, the most ever brought in a single case. The suspects were prosecuted under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.

Among those convicted on all charges was Mohamed Naufar, whom prosecutors identified as the ringleader who provided support to the eight-member suicide squad that carried out the bombings.

‘Mastermind’ spy boss

Three of the defendants were also charged by US authorities with terrorism-related offences linked to the bombings in December 2020. Five Americans were among those killed, including a US Commerce Department employee who was in Colombo on official business.

Other foreigners killed include citizens of Australia, Bangladesh, China, Denmark, India, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkiye and Britain.

The trial has unfolded against the backdrop of a separate and highly sensitive investigation into allegations that elements within the Sri Lankan state may have had links to those responsible for the attacks.

Former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is in custody facing accusations that he had been the “mastermind” who orchestrated the bombings, allegations he denies. Public Security Minister Ananda Wijepala told parliament in June that investigators believed he had worked with Islamist extremists before the bombings were carried out.

Investigators said the network was cultivated to manufacture a security threat that would in turn bolster political support for the Rajapaksa family, which returned to power several months after the attack with Gotabaya Rajapaksa’s election as president.

According to court filings, investigators believed the objective was to create chaos and present Rajapaksa, a former defence chief, as the leader best placed to restore security. Rajapaksa was credited by supporters with crushing Tamil separatist rebels in 2009 after a decades-long civil war.

Published in Dawn, September 23rd, 2026

item.title: AI will not kill us, suspicion will. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Since the beginning of this month, much of the international press have carried out the same story: Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old British researcher who spent three years on pretraining work at OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned on September 9 to sound a public alarm. He left two months before his Anthropic equity vested , forfeiting a massive corporate fortune to speak out.
Sitting opposite Anderson Cooper on CNN , Coxon revealed that the people building these frontier systems privately believe the technology could kill us all by the end of the decade, yet they are racing towards self-improving superintelligence regardless. Evan Hubinger, still inside the company, similarly estimates this existential risk above one in ten within the decade.
Crucially, Coxon made one point that most mainstream coverage missed: Today's systems are not an extinction threat. What frightens him is the sheer velocity at which they are beginning to improve themselves.
Warnings from these insider engineers deserve serious attention. But while Washington, Brussels, and San Francisco argue about a hypothetical intelligence explosion, Bangladesh has already experienced a much more real and immediate threat.
We do not need a sentient machine to damage our society. Everyday consumer software is already doing the work, and almost no one has noticed.
Anthropic’s report, published on September 10, describes a lone operator working from a laptop in Gaibandha. Over roughly 16 months, he ran 29 rotated Claude accounts through a custom Python script and produced, by the company's count, at least 1,500 Bengali headlines, 300 fabricated narratives, and 1,500 image prompts.
The content was designed to boost one specific political faction while systematically undercutting its rivals. Crucial context disappeared amid the immediate commentary. The company reports no evidence that any political group directed or funded the work. It also states that it could not establish how widely the material circulated.
These unverified findings come solely from one private firm's internal logs. What remains beyond question is the changing equation of deception, and that is the shift deserving our attention.
A propaganda line that once required a coordinated infrastructure of writers, editors, and designers can now be run by a single individual with a basic internet connection.
The cost of producing a plausible, grammatically-clean falsehood in Bangla has fallen close to zero. When fiction becomes free to manufacture while verification remains expensive, the public square tilts. It does not tilt back on its own.
For years, the standard response has been to ask whether we can detect the fake. That approach fails on simple mathematics. A producer can generate a fresh variant faster than any classifier or fact-checker can categorize the last one.
The local defensive line in that race remains dangerously thin. Digitally Right's election study counted roughly 40-50 professional fact-checkers for a country of more than 170 million people.
Most newsrooms lack a dedicated verification desk. The threat is not that individual citizens fall for fakes, but that synthetic saturation ruins collective trust in the public square.
When any image or audio can be flawlessly synthesized, the authority of genuine evidence collapses. A study in the American Political Science Review found that political deepfakes are not inherently more persuasive than ordinary text rumours, but politicians who falsely cry deepfake successfully protect their standing.
A 2026 experiment by researchers at Würzburg, published in Psychology of Popular Media , explained why this tactic works. The false claim dramatically raises the chance that viewers misidentify genuine footage as fabricated.
Legal scholars Bobby Chesney and Danielle Citron named this the liar's dividend . The terminal damage of generative AI is not that citizens believe lies, but that they lose the will to believe the truth.
That erosion is especially dangerous in Bangladesh, where the information environment is fragmented and crowded with anonymous pages and unverified forwards.
Around the February 2026 election, fact-checkers logged a surge of AI-generated material. Research by Digitally Right documented fabricated videos and synthetic images deployed against women candidates and minority communities.
In response, the Election Commission barred using AI tools to distort facts, mislead voters, or compromise electoral integrity.
The state's primary answer has been reactive removal. Following the passage of the Cyber Security Act in April 2026 , the government rapidly introduced draft amendments to force platforms to take down harmful AI-generated content within a fixed window.
The framework empowers the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission to block material and demand user data. The latest draft proposals reintroduce severe penalties, floating up to ten-year sentences for spreading rumours and disinformation online.
Rights groups, including Transparency International Bangladesh , have rightly warned that these sweeping changes risk a return to the repressive Digital Security Act era.
We now have a well-developed answer to one question: How do we take material down? Yet, we have almost no answer to another: How do we keep people believing material that is true?
The Draft National AI Policy 2026–2030 is not blind to this dilemma, explicitly emphasizing transparency, human oversight, and public trust.
Similarly, the Personal Data Protection Act covers the governance of data. But no statute can manufacture belief. A government can order a platform to remove a video, but it cannot order a citizen to trust the next one.
To heal this rift in trust, Bangladesh does not need faster censorship pipelines or wider legal nets. It needs a foolproof way to prove the creation of public-interest truth.
Rather than building a bloated, general-purpose AI regulator, the state should forge a tight, targeted national evidence chain for critical media.
For critical updates, like election tallies, official decrees, disaster warnings, public health guidelines, and state archives, institutions must publish digitally-signed media carrying tamper-proof source data straight from the point of origin.
News organizations should be supported, and for high-impact investigations eventually required, to preserve and display the original credentials of their footage. Platforms operating here should have to read those credentials and show users whether a circulating clip matches the signed original.
There is a real obstacle to admit: Most platforms re-encode uploads in ways that break the signature, so a duty to read credentials is worthless without a duty to preserve them. That is a negotiation with Meta, TikTok, or Google, not just a line printed in a state gazette. It should be the regulator's first demand.
Attribution, however, is no synonym for truth. An unedited video can still capture a politician telling a lie. It does not validate a narrative; it simply fixes the baseline.
It guarantees three basic facts:
That shifts the burden away from exhausting forensic guesswork, giving citizens, journalists, and courts solid ground to stand on.
None of this requires reinventing the wheel. The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity publishes an open standard, now in its fourth major revision , with Adobe, Microsoft, Google, OpenAI, Meta, the BBC, and the Associated Press, among thousands of members.
American cyber authorities recommended content credentials to government agencies in a 2025 advisory; Google Search surfaces the data, OpenAI attaches credentials to image outputs, and Leica, Nikon, Sony, and Canon ship cameras that sign at the shutter . Adoption is real but patchy. Bangladesh's task is integration, not invention.
The individuals most vulnerable to synthetic information are not the uneducated but the time-poor. A garment worker checking her phone after a long shift, a farmer reading a flash-flood alert, a first-time voter trying to understand a candidate’s speech.
None of them can run forensics on every file that reaches them. A democracy cannot expect its citizens to be part-time investigators.
Nor can we accept an ecosystem where any inconvenient piece of journalism is waved away as an AI-generated fake. The first danger is mass deception. The second is blanket cynicism, and it is harder to undo.
Leaving this suspicion unchecked also creates a profound sovereignty problem for governance. Frontier AI firms have become the de facto border police of global digital behaviour , detecting and disabling accounts they judge malicious.
Who decides what counts as a suspicious pattern when a Bangladeshi researcher or student queries a foreign-hosted model?
Digital sovereignty cannot be outsourced to a corporate board in California. Concurrently, it cannot mean that our domestic security apparatus inspects the private digital interactions of every citizen.
The only viable standard, which the draft policy introduces, is that any algorithmic decision materially affecting a Bangladeshi must be human-reviewable, fully auditable, and open to appeal.
This framework must govern the foreign enterprise services that power our economy, not merely public sector infrastructure.
It is deeply contradictory to obsess over existential risks, like whether a future machine will declare humanity obsolete, while failing to secure the foundational evidence by which society determines what is true in the present.
The initial casualty of the AI era will not be physical; it will be the consensus that evidence is final. Once that epistemic baseline is lost, it cannot be salvaged by a superior language model, an expedited fact-check, or a restrictive censorship order.
A democracy can endure intense ideological friction over its future. It cannot endure a total fracture regarding its past. Bangladesh must establish this mechanism today, before reality itself is reduced to a permanent question mark.
Dr Sabbir Ahmad, a tech executive with global experience in digital connectivity, sustainable infrastructure and energy, now shaping Bangladesh's semiconductor landscape as the CEO of Silicon Array Ltd. Email: sabbir@ieee.org.

item.title: The stranger is not always a stranger. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We teach children not to talk to strangers. We tell them not to accept food from unknown people, not to get into unfamiliar cars, and not to wander too far from home. It is useful advice, but it may also give adults a dangerously comforting picture of where childhood is unsafe.
The disturbing truth emerging from recent cases is that the person who poses a threat to a child may not look like a stranger at all. He may be a relative, a neighbour, an acquaintance, a family member, or someone the child has seen often enough to trust.
That should force us to reconsider how we understand child safety in Bangladesh. The problem is not simply that some children are murdered. It is that the systems designed to protect them often become active only after something terrible has already happened.
The numbers are difficult to ignore. Between January and July this year, 15,717 children were reported missing across the country, according to Police Headquarters. Of them, 13,679 were rescued or returned to their families, while 2,038 remained untraced.
Among those still missing were 68 children aged nine or below and 1,970 aged between 10 and 17. These figures do not tell us how many of those children ultimately faced violence, exploitation, or trafficking. But they establish something more fundamental: Disappearance is not a marginal problem.
Another set of figures makes the issue even more unsettling. According to monitoring by child-rights organization Shishurai Shob, 86 children were killed in 78 incidents during the first six months of this year. 46 of the victims were aged six or below.
More than half of the killings occurred within a family environment, including the victim's own home or the home of a relative. Parents were implicated in 17 cases, relatives in 11, and neighbours or acquaintances in 22.
The numbers should not be interpreted as proof that every family home is dangerous or that every parent, relative, or neighbour represents a threat. They do, however, challenge the simplistic idea that child protection is mainly about keeping children away from unknown outsiders. Familiarity can create trust, and trust can sometimes become the very condition that allows abuse or violence to remain invisible.
There is another uncomfortable lesson here. A child does not have to disappear for society to fail that child. Violence can happen behind a closed door, inside a familiar neighbourhood, or within a household that appears perfectly ordinary from outside. By the time the crime becomes visible, the opportunity to prevent it may already have disappeared.
This is why the first hours after a child goes missing deserve much greater attention. A missing child should not initially be treated as a routine missing-person complaint that can wait for the machinery of bureaucracy to start moving. The first hours can contain digital traces, phone locations, CCTV footage, online activity, financial transactions, and eyewitness memories that may disappear quickly. Delay is not neutral when evidence is disappearing by the minute.
Bangladesh therefore needs something more sophisticated than periodic campaigns telling parents to be careful. It needs a national missing-child response mechanism with clearly defined responsibilities, rapid information sharing and a standard emergency protocol.
Police, cybercrime units, telecommunications operators, local administration, and relevant child-protection organizations should not have to discover how to coordinate after every tragedy. The procedure should already exist.
Technology can help, but technology alone will not save children. A phone can be tracked, but someone must decide to track it quickly. CCTV can contain crucial evidence, but someone must collect and preserve it before it is overwritten. An online account may reveal a child's last movements, but someone must know which digital traces matter.
There is also a dangerous tendency to measure success by arrests. An arrest makes a headline. A confession makes another. But neither necessarily tells us whether the system worked.
If a child disappears, is found dead, and an accused person is arrested, we should not automatically call the case successfully resolved. We should also ask what happened during the hours between disappearance and recovery. Was the report acted upon immediately? Were digital records secured? Were relevant people questioned? Were search efforts coordinated? Were warning signs overlooked?
Justice begins after a crime, but child protection begins before it.
The same logic applies to the way we discuss family violence. When a child is killed by someone close to the family, the tragedy is often described as a shocking individual act. That may be true, but the individual explanation can sometimes conceal the social conditions surrounding the crime.
The first six months of this year saw 19 child killings linked in monitoring reports to anger or quarrels, 18 to rape, and 14 to abuse. In 13 cases, no specific reason could be identified from available reports.
These categories are not explanations in themselves, and the organization has rightly cautioned that they are based largely on preliminary media information. Yet they point towards a wider problem that cannot be solved through policing alone.
A society that wants to protect children must learn to recognize danger before violence becomes fatal. Domestic conflict, sexual abuse, coercion, threats, unexplained injuries, sudden behavioural changes, and repeated disappearances cannot always be dismissed as private family matters.
Schools, teachers, relatives, neighbours, and community organizations need channels through which concerns can be reported without exposing children to further danger.
There is also a question of what happens after the cameras leave. Shishurai Shob found reports of arrests in 44 of the 78 cases it monitored during January-June, while 14 contained no information about legal action.
Arrest statistics are not the same as convictions, and media monitoring cannot capture the entire judicial process. But the gap itself should concern us. A child who has been killed cannot be brought back by a successful prosecution. Yet accountability matters because impunity teaches society that some lives can be taken at a manageable cost.
Perhaps the most important change we need is conceptual. A missing child should not be treated merely as a child who has left a place. A missing child is a child whose whereabouts are unknown and whose safety is therefore uncertain. That distinction sounds small, but it changes everything. It changes how quickly authorities respond, how seriously evidence is preserved, and how institutions understand their responsibility.
We have become accustomed to asking who killed the child. We should also ask a harder question: What happened while the child was still alive and missing?
That is where prevention begins. And that is where a serious child-protection system must learn to look.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: No human rights without sign language rights. [ newagebd ]
item.description: ON SEPTEMBER 23, the world will mark the International Day of Sign Languages. For deaf people, this is not simply an annual observance. It is a reminder of something that should never have needed defending: sign languages are real, complex natural languages, and the people who use them are entitled to the same rights, dignity and opportunities as everyone else...

item.title: A deadly price for regulatory failure in Ashulia. [ newagebd ]
item.description: THE blast that killed eight people and injured more than 24 others at Ashulia in Dhaka exposes the grave risks of transporting and handling high-pressure CNG cylinders through an unsafe system. The explosion occurred at about 6:45pm on September 20 while cylinders were being unloaded from a covered van at S Suhi Industrial Park Ltd, part of Pretty Group at Jamgora. Fire Service officials said 12 covered vans were unloading cylinders, with each vehicle carrying around 90 cylinders...

item.title: The uncounted care economy. [ newagebd ]
item.description: FACTORIES, farms, exports, remittances, businesses and formal employment typically measure Bangladesh’s economy. Yet much of the country’s economic system operates outside these conventional measures: cooking, cleaning, caring for children, supporting older family members, caring for sick relatives and countless daily tasks that keep households functioning. Much of this work is unpaid, disproportionately performed by women and largely invisible in national economic calculations...
